newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Blair to press ahead with utilities tax.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Blair to press ahead with utilities tax.

text.p: Opposition leader Tony Blair vowed on Sunday to press ahead with plans for a special tax on Britain's privatised gas, electricity and water firms to pay for an attack on unemployment despite claims it could be illegal.

In a pre-election interview, Blair pledged that helping the young -- both jobless youths and those still at school -- to better lives will be the passion of the government he hopes to form within months.

"Unless we get our education system in this country right, we will not be prepared for a new economic world out there and we will never create the kind of just society we want to see," he said on BBC television.
Blair, whose party is some 20 points ahead of the ruling Conservatives with an election due by May 22, has promised not to increase the burden of taxation on ordinary Britons.

So to pay for plans to get the long-term unemployed and people under 25 into work, he wants to levy a "windfall profits tax" on the utility companies which he says have made unfair profits since being privatised by the Conservatives.
Although Labour has not put a figure on the sum to be raised from such a tax, some analysts believe it could be around five billion pounds ($8.5 billion) to help some 250,000 people.
The right-wing economic think-tank Aims of Industry said on Sunday top lawyers it had consulted had suggested such a tax would be illegal under European Union law.

"European law gives a number of rights to companies so that they should be treated fairly and equally. This would suggest Labour's proposals would be against the law," the group's director Michael Ivens told the Mail on Sunday newspaper.
But Blair said Labour had also taken legal advice on its plans which had been "very, very clear indeed".
He accused "a very well organised lobbying campaign" backed by the utilities and the Conservatives of trying to frustrate plans for the windfall tax.
"(They) want to go on the legal basis because they know that the plans themselves are perfectly popular," he said.
Blair went on to pledge that the first bill to be introduced into parliament by a Labour government would be one on education.
"That is because it is the absolute key to everything an incoming Labour government can hope to do," he said.
Meanwhile, the Independent on Sunday newspaper reported that the Conservatives were planning a further massive privatisation if they win the election.
It said a sell-off of London's underground railway system, with assets of 13 billion pounds ($22 billion), was likely to feature in the party's election manifesto.
